title: Divers Find What May Be the World’s Oldest Shipwreck
paragraphs: A research team led from Turkey says it has found what may be the oldest shipwreck known, lying in shallow water off Kekova, west of Antalya. The wreck is tentatively dated to about 2700–2400 BCE, or roughly 4,500 years ago, which would beat the previous record holder off Dokos in Greece by around three centuries.

Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University found the site in 2024, acting on clues from local seafarers. No timbers survive, but large storage jars, many with a raised clay belt, lie wedged in a rocky slope; divers spent about four months freeing them from barnacles. Some jars, or their clay, may have come from the Central Jordan Valley. Karin Sowada of Macquarie University, who writes about the find, calls what remains under the sea “a time capsule of ancient trade.”

The claims should be read with caution. The work has not been peer reviewed, the dating is provisional and earlier or later dates remain possible, and analysis of the residue, which could be olive oil, wine or tree resin, is unfinished. With so little of the hull left, the ship’s route is unknown; the authors suggest it was seeking shelter from a storm when it struck the rocks.

questions.q: How much older than the previous record would the wreck be?
How did Hakan Öniz find the site?
questions.a: By following clues from local seafarers.

questions.q: Why is the 4,500-year date still tentative?
questions.a: The work is not peer reviewed and earlier or later dates are possible.
